Chi Delta Installation
The Chi Delta was installed at
Duke University March 30, 1973.
The ceremony was conducted by
Brother Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21,
President of the Executive Council.
The following charter members of
Chi Delta were initiated: Peter Ed
win Broadbent, Jr. '73, Richmond,
Virginia; James Peter Carmody '73,
Rahway, New Jersey; Donald Wil
liam Goodman '73, Atlanta, Georgia;
Dale Gary Smith '73, Leesburg, Flori
da; Wilham Clarence Bost '74, Pinehurst, North Carolina; William Clarke
Fletcher, Jr. '74, Falls Church, Vir
ginia; Rufus Roberts Hambright, Jr.
'74, Greensboro, North Carolina;
Owen Arthur Jones '74, Vero Beach,
Florida; James Donald Klein '74,
Nashville, Tennessee; William Thom
as Lohmann '74, Massapequa, New
York; Steven Robert Savona '74, Bayside, New York; Philip Joseph Butera
'75, Brooklyn, New York; Joseph Ran
dolph Colahan '75, Garden City, New
York; Marilyn Hamilton '75, Orlando,
Florida; Clarence Douglas Henard,
Jr. '75, Nashville, Tennessee; Stephen
Decker Swank '75, Edmond, Okla
homa; Robert Lawrence Taylor, Jr.
'75, Fieldale, Virginia; James White
Caudill '76, Charleston, West Vir
ginia.
The following members of the Ex
ecutive Council attended the Installa
tion: Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21, Presi
dent; Robert W. Morey, Pi '20, VicePresident; John W. White, Jr., Chi
'28, Vice-President; Henry B. Poor,
Gamma '39, Secretary; William H.
Ducker, Phi '44; John E. Fricke, Xi
'23; and William R. Robie, Epsilon
Omega '66.
Brothers from four undergraduate
chapters attended: Mark I. Nickerson,
Xi '75; Howard M. DeLaittre, Beta
Beta '74; Robert E. Ward, Epsilon
Omega '75, President; David D.
Donel, Nu Alpha '75; Andrew G.
Hollinger, Nu Alpha '73; John A.
Syvertsen, Nu Alpha '74, President.
Also in attendance were the follow
ing Brothers: Peter A. Howley, Delta
'62; Paul J. Hughes, Delta '34; Don
ald M. Monson, Rho '51; and Robert
L. Titley, Phi '70.
In addition the following persons
were present at the Installation Ban
quet: Dean James E. Douthat, Assist
ant Dean of Students; Chesley Goldston, Chi Delta Phi '71; and Larry
W. Mobley, Chi Delta Phi '72.
At the Installation Banquet Brother
William R. Robie, Epsilon Omega '66,
was the very effective Master of Cere
monies. Greetings from the new chap
ter were extended by Brother Dale
C. Smith, Chi Delta '73, President;
and from Duke University by Dean
James E. Douthat, Assistant Dean of
Students. Brother John E. Fricke, Xi
'23, led the singing with his custom
ary skill. The address on "Responsi
bilities of Psi Upsilon Brotherhood,"
was delivered by President Albert C.
Jacobs, Phi '21. A few of his remarks
were as follows:
Brother Toastmaster, Brothers of
the Executive Council, our new
Brothers of Chi Delta, Brothers in
Psi Upsilon, and distinguished guests,
I am thrilled to take part in this
never-to-be-forgotten occasion, adorn
ing as it does the diadem of Psi Upsi
lon with a new and a brilliant dia
mond.
Psi Upsilon is extremely proud to
install the Chi Delta Chapter, our
third in the South, following the Nu
Alpha at Washington and Lee Uni
versity, and the Gamma Tau at the
Georgia Institute of Technology. For
the Chi Delta we have the highest ex
pectations. We are proud to install a
chapter at this outstanding institution
of higher learning which long has
stood for excellence in education, an
institution which has recognized the
meaningful service which fraternities
under proper conditions can render
Alma Mater. Psi Upsilon warmly wel
comes the privileged opportunity ef
fectively to cooperate with Duke Uni
versity in serving our youth.
Psi Upsilon is exceedingly proud
to welcome into the bonds of our So
ciety the eighteen splendid members
of Chi Delta: four seniors, seven jun
iors, six sophomores and one fresh
man, who reside in ten different
states. We greet you from the heart
and wish our Brothers of Chi Delta
of today and tomorrow Godspeed, the
greatest success, and enduring pros
perity. May you never regret the fra
ternal bonds into which you have en
tered today.
Psi Upsilon is particularly honored
over the way in which Chi Delta Phi
became a chapter of our Fraternity.
Founded in January 1968, "to create
a small close-knit yet diverse group
that while selective would be fair in
choosing members," from the outset
you were interested in joining a na
tional fraternity. To this most impor
tant decision you gave extremely
careful consideration. You very wise
ly took your time. You rejected a
number of well-established fraterni
ties that were genuinely interested.
Psi Upsilon came into the picture in
early 1970. We at once saw your
great potential, but refrained from ap
plying any pressure. We gave you ev
ery opportunity to learn about us, and
to choose the society with which you
wished to associate. When your deci
sion was finally made in January of
this year, it was completely voluntary
on your part, in accordance with the
best traditions of our Fraternity.
You have received an unparalleled
heritage, the firmest of foundations.
In receiving this heritage, you have
assumed responsibilities for "the pro
motion of the highest moral, intellec
tual and social excellence." Yours is
the beginning now of a larger en
deavor, the commencement of added
responsibility. Never forget, one must
give in order to receive. Rights and
privileges are meaningless unless we
are willing to fight for them.
The need is greater than ever for
the ideals which our Founders so
wisely propounded. In this day of
revolutionary change and of amazing
upheaval, there is a telling demand
for persons with "a clear and worthy
view of life," for persons of dyna
mism, talent and imagination; persons
of character, integrity and ability,
who have the guts to defend their
ideals, the heritage they have re
ceived, who have the courage, the
conviction to speak out articulately
in an orderly fashion for what they
believe, for the values they dearly
prize.
Yes, Brothers, you have today as
sumed heavy responsibilities, but
their effective and meaningful fulfill
ment will be rich in accomplishment,
will open to you new horizons, will
make you far better citizens and lead
ers of our beloved Country. God
speed to you as you enter our Broth
erhood.
Until the end of time may Chi
Delta and Duke University serve our
youth, promoting "the highest moral,
intellectual and social excellence,"
providing the citizens and leaders our
country and the world so direly need.
It has been wonderful to be with
you tonight, to participate in welcom
ing Chi Delta into our beloved Fra
ternity; to hear again the good old
songs.
"Until the sands of life are run.
We'll sing to thee, Psi Upsilon."

130th Convention of The
Psi Upsilon Fraternity
The 130th Convention will be held
with the Gamma Chapter at Amherst
College in Amherst, Massachusetts,
from Sunday evening, August 26,
through Wednesday evening, August
29. Regional Conferences, voted last
year to be continued annually as well,
will precede the 130th Convention,
starting Saturday evening, August 25,
1973.
The Convention Committee con
sists of the following: Earl W. Mer
rill, Gamma '27, General Chairman;
Philip H. Ball, Jr., Gamma '40; Rob
ert L. Beatty, Jr., Gamma '73; Miner
D. Crary, Jr., Gamma '42; Albert C.
Jacobs, Phi '21; John W. Keene, Jr.,
Gamma '72; Henry B. Poor, Gamma
'39; Christopher G. Rafferty, Gamma
'74; Christopher Winslow, Gamma
'74.
At the Convention each chapter is
entitled to representation by two of
ficially accredited undergraduate del
egates and one officially accredited
alumni delegate. In addition, other
undergraduate and alumni Brothers
are cordially invited and warmly en
couraged to attend all Regional Con
ference and Convention functions.
The Convention is the most impor
tant single event in the Psi Upsilon
spectrum. Upon decisions voted at
each Convention rest the policies and
actions of the Fraternity until the fol
lowing Convention.
Where the Convention serves as
the Fraternity's basic legislative chan
nel. Regional Conferences provide a
unique opportunity for extended dis
cussion of concerns common to chap
ters in the same geographical area.
The results of their deliberations will
comprise the core of the Convention
agenda.
For a number of months the Con
vention Committee has been hard at
work to make this occasion one of the
most memorable in Psi Upsilon his
tory. The Central Office urgently
needs and requests cooperation in re
gard to the following matters :
1. An early designation of officially
accredited delegates. Nothing is more
important than that every chapter be
represented, and that every chapter
be represented by a fuU complement
of two undergraduate delegates and
one alumni delegate.
2. The return of preliminary infor
mation for all who are coming. At
tendance by official delegates for the
full period, from Saturday, August 25,
through Wednesday, August 29, can
not be emphasized too strongly.
Events have been scheduled to limit
the loss of business or work time to
three days and to close well in ad
vance of the Labor Day weekend.
3. The preparation of a written re
port by the undergraduates of each
chapter, replacing the oral reports at
previous Conventions, to be repro
duced collectively and mailed to all
delegates in advance of the Conven
tion. The report need not be long, but
should include membership statistics,
academic and campus standing, finan
cial condition, unique features, high
lights of the past year, and principal
concerns.
All business sessions, the workshop.
Regional Conference sessions and
committee meetings will be in Con
verse Hall, an Amherst administrative
building, except for the Executive
Council Meeting Sunday evening at
the Gamma Chapter House. All dele
gates will be housed in one of the
dormitories on the Amherst College
campus. All lunches and dinners will
be in a designated dining room of
Valentine Hall, except for the Sunday
noon picnic at Rolling Hill Farm and
the Sunday evening steak barbecue
at the Gamma Chapter. Doughnuts
and coffee will be served each morn
ing at Converse Hall and the Gamma
Chapter House.
A package charge of eighty-five
dollars for each undergraduate and
ninety-five dollars for each alumnus
will cover all expenses for the Region
al Conferences and the Convention;
seventy dollars for undergraduates
and eighty dollars for alumni will
cover the Convention. Individual
charges for registration, meals, and
accommodations also will be available
for Brothers who can attend only a
portion of the proceedings.
Converse Hall. Convention Business Sessions and Committee Meetings
will be held in Amherst's former Library, recently remodeled to house
administrative offices and seminar rooms.

From the President's Desk
I am extremely happy to report
that for the second consecutive year
all of our undergraduate chapters
have been visited officially. I person
ally have had the privilege of visiting
nineteen of our twenty-eight chapters.
Brother Henry B. Poor, Gamma '39,
Secretary of the Executive Council,
has done yeoman's work in regard to
our visitations. I am deeply grateful
to Brother Robert W. Morey, Pi '20,
Vice President of the Executive
Council, for his splendid help.
These visitations were an eminently
satisfying experience. It was singular
ly encouraging to talk with our spendid young members across the coun
try. With a very few exceptions I was
very happily impressed with the
strength of our chapters as well as
with the revitalization of the fraterni
ty movement on our many campuses.
I am extremely proud to be a mem
ber of Psi Upsilon, currently to be in

Psi Upsilon is not a wealthy Fra
ternity. Its endowment is very small.
Its Central Office is run on a most
economical basis. The Executive
Council depends to a very large ex

dues and chapter taxes for effective
operation. The support of all loyal
members of our Fraternity will be
sincerely appreciated.
Psi Upsilon is not standing on the
laurels of yesterday. Since November
6, 1970, three splendid new chapters
of our Fraternity have been installed:
The Nu Alpha at Washington and
Lee University, the Gamma Tau at
the Georgia Institute of Technology,
and on March 30, 1973 the Chi Delta
at Duke University. Psi Upsilon is
anxious to install further chapters at
Townsend '76, Robert J. Vavrina '76,
and Jeffery M. Walck '75.
An inspirational charge was given
in the Chapter Room by William H.
Hall, Upsilon '72. After the formal
ceremony the initiates joined the
Brothers and many alumni in attend
ance for pre-dinner cocktails. Follow
ing the banquet Theodore A. Nist '73,
as toastmaster, proceeded to intro
duce Nicholas B. Brown, Upsilon '28,
and Russell "Woodchuck" Sherman
'70, guest of honor. Alumni represent
atives Richard D. Sherwood '56, and
Richard E. Rice '65, found it difficult
to top their words of wisdom but
were well received.
President James M. Dunnigan '73,
and Pledge Father Francis R. Moulin
'74, spoke for the Chapter. Brother
Moulin's elocution was particularly
impressive. The annual pledge awards
were presented at this time, with Da
vid R. Moller '75, winning the aca
demic award and Mitchell Reichman
'76, receiving the Burritt Award as
the outstanding pledge.
The evening reached its high point
with the address by the principal
speaker, Gardner A. Callanen, Jr., Psi
'29, of Utica, New York. Brother Cal
lanen is a member of the Executive
Council and the vice-president of The
well-established colleges and univer
sities. The office will welcome recom
mendations in this regard.
I hope sincerely that as many
Psi U's as possible will attend the
130th Convention to be held with the
Gamma at Amherst College August
26, 27, 28, and 29, 1973. A number
of very important decisions will be
before this Convention. The Conven
tion will be preceded by Regional
Conferences.
I have complete confidence in the
future of Psi Upsilon provided the
Executive Council has sufficient finan
cial resources effectively to handle its
operations as well as the strong lead
ership necessary wisely to direct Psi
Upsilon.
With every good wish,
Yours in the Bonds,
Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21

sides in Enfield, New Hampshire. He

Donald A. Finkbeiner, Phi '17
By Albert C. Jacobs, Phi '21
Psi Upsilon and the Phi have lost
one of their most distinguished, de
voted and loyal members. Brother
Finkbeiner, who lived alone, was
found dead in his home April 30,
1973. Death was attributed to inter
nal hemorrhaging.
A native of Perrysburg, Ohio, he
was the son of one of the oldest and
most respected families in Wood
County. The family had a tradition
dating back before the Civil War of
Presbyterianism and Republicanism,
and Brother Finkbeiner followed
both.
Brother Finkbeiner was graduated
from the old Toledo Central High
School in 1912. He then attended the
University of Michigan until 1917,
when he enlisted in the army. He re
sumed his studies at Michigan follow
ing the War, receiving both his bach
elor's and law degrees. He passed the
Ohio Bar in 1920.
Brother Finkbeiner gained wide
recognition in connection with his in
dustrial, business, and utility legal
work throughout the United States.
For four years Brother Finkbeiner
was associated with the firm of Tracy,
Chapman and Welles in Toledo. In
1924 he began representing Commu
nity Traction, and in 1927 moved his
offices into the headquarters of the
company, where they remained until
1939.
Brother Finkbeiner then practiced
alone until 1952, when he formed a
partnership with Joseph D. Stecher.
From 1958 through 1968 he was a
partner of Charles E. Ide, Jr. Since
then he had practiced alone.
The civic achievements he counted
during a colorful legal career which
spanned fifty-three years were numer
ous. He served on the Toledo Metro
politan Park District since 1946, and
was named its president in 1965, a
post he held at the time of his death.
He had been a member of the Toledo
Zoological Society since 1936, and a
member of the Zoo board of man
agers, the governing body, since
1952.
Brother Finkbeiner was president
of the Zoological Society from 1969
through 1971.
He also was a leader in the legal
community, having served as presi
dent of the Ohio State Bar Associa
tion in 1940 and 1941. He was a
member of the board of governors of
the American Bar Association, and
served on its House of Delegates and
as a state delegate from Ohio. From
1937 to 1940' he served on the execu
tive committee of the Toledo Bar As
sociation.
He also was a member of the
American Law Institute, American
Judicature Society, and a charter
member of the World Peace Through
Law Center.
Brother Finkbeiner was exceeding
ly active in civic and community af
fairs. At the time of his death Brother
Finkbeiner was a trustee of the Boys'
Club of Toledo, having been named
in 1946; a director of the Toledo So
ciety for Crippled Children, a post he
held for more than twenty-five years;
and on the advisory board of the Sal
vation Army.
In 1945, Brother Finkbeiner was
chairman of the American Red Cross
War Fund drive in the Toledo area.
He also served as president of the
Tuberculosis Society of Toledo and
Lucas County in 1967. He was on the
society's board from 1951 through
1972. He served as chairman of the
Toledo Christmas Seal campaign in
1949 and 1950.
In the 1950's Brother Finkbeiner
was chairman of the law committee
of the American Transit Association;
a trustee of the Maumee Valley Coun
try Day School as well as a trustee of
the Toledo Automobile Club.
Brother Finkbeiner was a member
of the Rotary Club of Toledo, the
Toledo Club, Toledo Country Club,
University Club of New York and
Columbus, the Columbus Athletic
Club, the Press Club of Ohio, the
Toledo Area and Ohio Chamber of
Commerce, and the American Legion.
He was a member and former trustee
of the Collingwood Presbyterian
Church.
For three score and one years
Brother Finkbeiner was a tower of
great strength to Psi Upsilon and to
the Phi. His loss will be deeply felt
by our Fraternity and by his beloved
chapter which he served so long, and
with such constructive dedication.
Brother Finkbeiner was long "Mr.
Phi," the chapter's outstanding alum
nus. For many years he was a highly
valued member of the Phi Alumni
Corporation, serving for eleven years
as the most respected President.
Brother Finkbeiner rendered nota
ble service to Psi Upsilon and the
Phi. He was the extremely able Chair
man of the 1956 Convention with the
Phi as the host. He was the highly
successful General Chairman of the
never-to-be forgotten Centennial of
the Phi in January of 1965. He was
the Honorary Chairman of the 129th
Convention in 1972 with the Phi
again as host. He was extremely help
ful in planning this Convention. At
the time of his death he was an hon
orary director of The Psi Upsilon
Foundation, Inc.
He is survived by a son and a
daughter.

Chester A. Arthur, who succeeded
to the presidency after James A. Gar
field was assassinated, was principal
of the school in Vermont. Much of
Arthur's boyhood was spent in Capitaland where he attended schools in
Washington County and in Schenec
tady, graduated from Union College
and taught school in Schaghticoke
and Cohoes.
Chester Arthur moved with his
family from Fairfield, Vt., to Union
Village (now Greenwich) in Wash
ington County in 1839. His father,
the Rev. William Arthur had become
pastor of the Baptist Church there.
The young Arthur attended an acade
my in Union Village run by James I.
Laurie, a graduate of Union.
Laurie, who became a prominent
attorney in the town, recalled the
youth in a letter to an editor of a
newspaper: "Another scholar of those
days, though only about 12 years of
age, was Chester A. Arthur. His eyes
were dark and brilliant, and his phys
ical system finely formed. He was
frank and open in manners and genial
in his disposition.
"Even at that early age he was a
favorite with all who knew him. He
was full of life and animation. His ac
tive abilities, his courage and his
strength of will made him a leader
among his companions.
"One of his sisters, an excellent and
beautiful girl, died here at the old
Baptist parsonage where the Rev. Dr.
Arthur presided. He (Chester) after
wards graduated at Union College,
and settled in the city of New York,
and distinguished himself as a lead
ing and reliable statesman,"
In his "Chester A, Arthur," George
F. Howe relates a story told by a boy
hood friend of Arthur: "When Ches
ter was a boy, you might see him in
the village street after a shower,
watching boys building a mud dam
across the rivulet in the roadway.
Pretty soon he would be ordering one
to bring stones, another sticks, and
others sod and mud to finish the dam;
and they would all do his bidding
without question. But he took good
care not to get any of the dirt on his
hands."
Chester A. Arthur, Theta 1848
Howe also tells the story of what
was probably Arthur's first political
triumph in the election of 1844, Ar
thur and other youthful supporters
of Henry Clay erected an "ash pole"
in Union Village in honor of their
candidate. Backers of James Polk,
Clay's Democratic rival, attempted to
topple the pole. The Whigs battled
them off and Arthur thus received his
first taste of political victory.
Moving to Schenectady in 1844,
Arthur attended the Lyceum, prepar
ing for college in the modernistic (for
its time) three-story octagonal build
ing at Union and Yates streets.
When he was 15, he entered Union
College as a sophomore, enrolling in
the traditional "Classical Course."
Among his studies were algebra and
geometry, moral and natural philoso
phy, physiology and the works of
Livy, Homer and Xenophon. At the
age of 18, Arthur graduated Phi Beta
Kappa, one of six to be so honored
in a class of more than 100.
His graduation from Union while
so young seems even more remarkable
in that he took two winters off from
college to teach school. Because he
needed money to pay for his studies,
Arthur became an instructor at dis
trict school No. 14 in Schaghticoke
in Rensselaer County. According to
Howe, Arthur was paid $18 a month
in 1848.
After Union, Arthur attended a law
school in Ballston Spa for several
months. He then went to live with his
father in Lansingburgh to study law
at home.
In 1851 he became principal of the
academy in North Pownal, Vt., where
three years later Garfield was to be
come an instructor. Arthur left Pow
nal in 1853, returning to Capitaland
to become principal of an academy
in Cohoes.
Howe describes Arthur's experience
in Cohoes: "There he completed the
studies which qualified him for ad
mission to a lawyer's office and made
a record as a principal which won
him the esteem of the community.
Upon taking over the school, he
taught the 'high department,' in
which a rowdy bunch of boys had tri
umphed over several of his predeces
sors. He was warned that disciphne
would be his greatest problem.
"His first act was to explain to the
class that he knew its reputation and
intended to deal fairly but firmly with
every misdemeanor. With consider
able resourcefulness, Arthur eventual
ly gained complete mastery of the en
tire department,"
Arthur left Capitaland to begin a
law career in New York City where
he joined the firm of a friend of the
family, Erastus D, Culver. Culver had
been a Congressman from Washing
ton County.
Roscoe Conkling, who dominated
the Republican party for several dec
ades, found in Arthur an able lieu
tenant, Arthur became collector of the
port of New York, a key position for
its patronage power, and a prominent
member of the "Stalwart" wing of the
GOP. When the Republicans asked
him to run with Garfield, in 1880,
Conkling did not look favorably on
Arthur's acceptance.
As an influential Republican, Ar
thur returned to Albany on two cam
paigns which were both interrupted
by dramatic events in his life.
In January, 1881, he was in Albany
on behalf of a friend. Gen. George
Sharpe of Kingston, who was seeking
the speakership of the state assembly.
While working to muster support for
Sharpe, Arthur received word of his
wife's being taken ill. He returned to
New York City but Mrs. Arthur died
within 24 hours. She was buried in
Albany Rural Cemeteiy. Her coffin
was met at the railroad station by
Gov. Alonzo Cornell and representa
tives of the Legislature. They escort
ed the cortege through the streets of
Albany by sleigh to the cemetery.
As vice president of the United
States, Arthur returned during the
summer of the same year in support
of Conkling and Thomas Piatt, who
had resigned from the U.S. Senate.
Both expected the state legislature to
re-elect them but despite Arthur's in
tercession, they were replaced. On
July 2, while Arthur was in Albany,
Garfleld was shot. Arthur became
president upon Garfield's death in
September.
Much to the dismay of his former
political allies, the Civil Service Re
form Act was passed under the ad
ministration of Chester Arthur.
He served until 1885 losing the
GOP nomination to James G. Blaine.
